positive.original:
Anyone who starts playing Stardew Valley and gets deeper into it will most certainly hear a phrase so often that they’ll maybe start to get a bit sick of it and hopefully even begin to question it: “there’s no wrong way to play the game.”
And yea, I get what people mean by that, but with this review I want to give new players some honest advice, don’t take that statement too literally. But first off and this is really important to me, I absolutely adore Stardew Valley. It’s very close to a perfect game and to get straight to the point, Stardew Valley is one of the sweetest, most heartfelt games and overall one of the best games I’ve ever played. It’s almost impossible not to notice how much passion and dedication went into making it.

There are games you absolutely want to play right at release, games that seem to need the right moment before you pick them up and games you follow for a long time where, even though you spend a lot of time looking into them, you’re still not sure if you’ll ever actually play them yourself, and that last one was exactly the case for me. Even though Eric Barone aka ConcernedApe, always came across to me as a very down-to-earth, humble and genuinely interesting person, I ended up waiting 10 years. But now I can happily say, better late than never. Also remarkable and in more than one way, is that Eric never held back from mentioning how much his wife/girlfriend/partner contributed to the project, supporting him through all the difficulties and always believing in him, while at the same time working two jobs to cover their shared living expenses. The two of them took a huge risk back then. Eric’s self-doubt could have consumed him or their relationship could have fallen apart. But despite all that, they made it through together and gave so many people a game that’s loved universally.

Anyone who’s really into video games has either already played Stardew Valley, is still playing it or at least has it on their radar and will very likely play it at some point. The most helpful tip I can give to newcomers comes from my own initial misjudgment. I thought I could lean back a bit more with this game, maybe take a few notes here and there about what to do next, but overall have a calm cozy experience where I could just switch my brain off. So, advice number one: use the game’s wiki right from the start and be prepared for it to feel like work at times, it can even get a bit stressful.
Second tip: don’t get frustrated with your first sprinkler or with fishing. It really does get better later on, even though those are definitely fair points to criticize. Next tip is for those of you who want to unlock all achievements. That currently doesn’t work if you’re in a same-sex relationship, because unfortunately it’s not possible to adopt children in the game, which is a real shame and something that should have been considered. There are a few more but one last tip here: don’t get annoyed when after getting the horse, you can’t ride over certain small flat stones or when you can’t get past your pet or in some tight spots, or when birthday characters you want to gift aren’t where the wiki says they should be. Like I said, it’s an almost perfect game.

Alongside shaping up your grandfather’s farm however you want, getting to know the world around it and its diverse characters, beating up monsters in the mines and searching for treasure, you’re accompanied by a soundtrack that plays a huge part in why Stardew Valley became such a success.
Eric who used to play in both a metal band and an experimental pop band, clearly knew exactly what a game like this needs and how to bring it to life. It’s not just built on solid music theory and well-crafted harmonies, it also has its own unique touch and a certain sense of freshness to it.
Depending on the season, the tracks feel a bit warmer or cooler. In the mines the music builds tension, while in the saloon, ragtime piano paired with the clinking of cutlery and glasses in the background creates a feeling of pure ease. No matter the situation or special event, each track delivers exactly the right emotion for the scene. I wouldn’t be surprised if a lot of players have shed a few tears during the Festival of the Moonlight Jellies ;  ))
So it’s also no surprise there are live orchestral concerts of the soundtrack. I’d honestly love to experience that in person but more than anything, I really want that double vinyl.

Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve got to get back to my farm, I forgot to refill the cat’s water and I should also check in on my mango orchard, over on Ginger Island while trying to track down the last five golden walnuts. The Luau is coming up as well and I still need to prepare a few things for that, especially since it’s 2:00 AM before you even realize it.

Edit (04/04/2026)

Made a mistake here but thankfully someone caught it and pointed it out to me. It is actually possible to adopt children. No idea how I ended up on the wrong track there, but in the end it’s on me for not properly checking the wiki. The only thing I remember is that I looked into adoption when I got to know Leo on Ginger Island better and started wondering if it might be possible to adopt him (which unfortunately isn’t). Maybe that’s where I got mixed up.
So yea sorry about that and just to clear it up once again, adoption is possible. Unfortunately, you just kind of have to rely on the wiki for everything.

Alright, still good news! Guess I’ll build a kids’ room and dig the crib out of storage again.

stardew is in my top 5 for favorite games. no matter how many times i replay it; it never loses it's charm. HOWEVER i'd like to speak to the person who said this was a "cozy game". this is one of the most stressful farming games i've ever seen. from getting attacked by 6 serpents in the skull caverns, trying to beat lewis's high score in junimo kart, being greedy and staying in the mines knowing it's almost 2am to finding an auto-petter and needing an entire wiki page open while you play. none of that screams cozy to me

and yet i still love this game 10/10

positive.original:
[h1] Pigs are more productive than dogs [/h1] 

That's the biggest impression the game left on me. 

I think a lot of info people would already be on the loop, I've played the game with extended version which adds some interesting chars and doesn't disable achievements(i would recommend it for what it's worth too).

I never played it before/at launch, 'cause I was waiting for a coop experience? In the end played it as singleplayer, it was very interesting to play blindly and 1.6 update has different approaches vanilla or modded, you don't need a vineyard META to get rich, you can become rich af with PIGS/Fishes/bees without having to do the excel min-maxing IQ usage. 

Granted I've found fish to be the most profitable and aesthetic wise, as each legendary fish changes the color of the Fish Ponds...bringing profit and beauty to the farm at the same time. Again it's your own choice how to get your money going to build your farm/family, but it's nice nowadays we have different options besides wine maxing to generate wealth for the farm :) . 

I presume coop has extra positives points but i can't write on those as of now. Def recommend for the singleplayer experience and would think the multiplayer one would be the best approach specially with SVE

positive.original:
Stardew Valley is one of those rare games that feels simple at first but slowly becomes something you can sink hundreds of hours into without even realizing it.

At its core, it’s a farming simulator—you inherit a run-down farm and build it up however you want. You plant crops, raise animals, mine for resources, fish, and craft items. But what really makes the game stand out is how much freedom it gives you. There’s no “right” way to play. You can focus on making the most efficient farm possible, or just spend your days fishing by the river and talking to townspeople.

The town itself is full of personality. Each character has their own routines, backstories, and relationships, which makes interacting with them feel meaningful rather than repetitive. As you get to know them, you unlock events that add emotional depth—some are lighthearted, while others touch on more serious themes like loneliness or personal growth.

Visually, the pixel art style is charming and timeless. It doesn’t try to be flashy, but it’s incredibly detailed and cozy. Paired with a relaxing soundtrack, the whole experience feels calm and comforting—perfect for unwinding after a long day.

One of the game’s biggest strengths is its progression system. There’s always something to work toward, whether it’s upgrading your tools, expanding your farm, completing bundles, or exploring deeper levels of the mines. Yet it never feels overly stressful unless you make it that way.

That said, it’s not perfect. The early game can feel a bit slow, especially when you’re low on energy and resources. Some mechanics aren’t explained very clearly, which might be confusing for new players, however these are minor issues compared to everything the game does right.

Overall, Stardew Valley is a relaxing, rewarding, and deeply engaging experience. Whether you’re into farming sims or just want a peaceful game to get lost in, it’s easy to recommend. It’s the kind of game you don’t just play—you live in it for a while.

But what really makes the game stand out is how much freedom it gives you. There’s no “right” way to play. You can focus on making the most efficient farm possible, or just spend your days fishing by the river and talking to townspeople.

The town itself is full of personality. Each character has their own routines, backstories, and relationships, which makes interacting with them feel meaningful rather than repetitive. As you get to know them, you unlock events that add emotional depth—some are lighthearted, while others touch on more serious themes like loneliness or personal growth.

Visually, the pixel art style is charming and timeless. It doesn’t try to be flashy, but it’s incredibly detailed and cozy. Paired with a relaxing soundtrack, the whole experience feels calm and comforting—perfect for unwinding after a long day.

One of the game’s biggest strengths is its progression system. There’s always something to work toward, whether it’s upgrading your tools, expanding your farm, completing bundles, or exploring deeper levels of the mines. Yet it never feels overly stressful unless you make it that way.

That said, it’s not perfect. The early game can feel a bit slow, especially when you’re low on energy and resources. Some mechanics aren’t explained very clearly, which might be confusing for new players, however these are minor issues compared to everything the game does right.

Overall, Stardew Valley is a relaxing, rewarding, and deeply engaging experience. Whether you’re into farming sims or just want a peaceful game to get lost in, it’s easy to recommend. It’s the kind of game you don’t just play—you live in it for a while.

I picked this up mainly because I love pixel games, and yeah, the art is great—but I didn’t expect to get this into it.

It starts off simple, just farming and figuring things out, but then you slowly get attached to everything. Your farm, the routines, even the villagers. I kept telling myself “just one more day” and suddenly hours were gone.

Came for the pixel art, stayed because it somehow became part of my daily routine.

I love playing the game with mods, getting the new game thrill over an over again. I know for a fact there is stuff I still dont know and I am truly happy for it.

Play Stardew and do chaos. No need for other stuff, make your friends annoyed by how much you play this game. I sure do annoy them lol.

positive.original:
I don't know how many consoles I've played this on or how many times I've bought it, but it is definitely a must have for any farming sim lover. 
The fact that one person basically put out this whole game by himself is absolutely bonkers!
I do wish there were more romanceable NEW partners introduced, not just rehashing old villagers to fit that criteria later on. Or more biomes/parts of the world would be neat. But I feel like I should just be happy that this game is still being tended to 10 years after being released. My favourite part of the game is how you can pick different settings for your farm at the beginning, it's really original and makes different play-throughs fun.
Overall it's a pretty well fleshed out game and I would consider it a classic at this point. Cozy, easy, and the world is your oyster.

This is one of my favorite games, and I don't ever see that changing.

I got it on sale because i saw other people play it and talk about how much they love the game, but after playing it for an hour or so I just didn't get it. It was only after playing it for a few hours more did it start to click why people like it so much.
It's a game about choices and time management. There will be many thing you may want to do, but the steps to get what you need can only be done at certain times and/or seasons, meaning if you miss a narrow window you'll need to remember next time - which could be an entire game year. 
This aspect drew me in, but the character of the storytelling and environment is what eventually kept me.

positive.original:
Stardew Valley is one of the best games of all time, there's so much content that time passes as if it was nothing. I had multiple sessions where I load in with the plans to only play for 2 hours and I end up spending 8 and that's what makes this game beautiful. The characters that you interact with have their own individual stories progressing as you do, the story is very simple to understand but it runs super deep. This game isn't just a farming simulator it's a life simulator, you build relationships with the villagers and you see their characters change as you become more friendly with them. The mining and combat in this game is oddly satisfying and feels rewarding, you need to harness every aspect of this game to get perfection.
The characters are all lovable (even Shane) once you start to understand their character.
If you haven't played this game yet you should absolutely play it, even if you think the game isn't for you there is aspects of this game for you.

positive.original:
Eric Barone — I'd kiss that dev's hands. Dude dropped a magnum opus and made a game you can disappear into for months. I bought it ages ago, played 5–6 hours with a friend, and it didn't click at all. Like, you just walk around, meet villagers, go mining, fish endlessly — huge mistake. Came back 2–3 years later, started a new save, and literally couldn't stop. Fishing, mining, building relationships, grinding achievements — all of it. The game is genius, and I'll recommend it to anyone. The main thing? It's kind. Like, genuinely kind. But at the same time, there's so much depth once you start digging into the villagers' stories.

Anyway, this game instantly got under my skin. I went for perfection, put in 200+ hours, and don't regret a single one. Literally everyone should play Stardew Valley — get lost in the story, the gameplay, and just how beautiful the world is. Oh, and the music? Absolute banger. 10/10, recommend.

positive.original: I've always disregarded/ignored farming sims and the like. I've been familiar with SDV for years and finally picked it up on sale....and I was hooked from the opening of the game! I had to force myself to delete the game at around 170 hours as I was finding every excuse in the book to spend my free time playing it. I wouldn't consider myself a newfound fan of the genre and I may never play another farming sim in my lifetime (unless it's more SDV ha ha). But Stardew is a special, lovingly crafted game in my opinion. Anyone that hasn't played this and is looking for a change of pace in their gaming diet should give this one a hard look first.

positive.original:
I feel like a glowing review of this game is unnecessary. It's a game that the vast majority of people who like these games, loves. 
That being said, I did not LOVE it at first. I know, blasphemy. It was hard for me at first because I was very much a Harvest Moon nerd for decades prior to giving Stardew an honest shot. Its a very similar but very different game. 
It came to head when I was home for an extended period of time with a big move.  I gave it the time it deserves, and found the love for it that I had been missing. 
This review is getting long winded and cheesy but in closing, Stardew is my palate cleanser game. It's amazing for the drive it requires and the the simplicity of exiting. It's also amazing on the my deck. :3

positive.original:
I've been meaning to write this for a while, because as you can see, I have 101 hours played in this game. That alone should tell you how good the game is, lol. After all, if you didn't like the game, why play that long, right? Anyways! This game has so much too it, that it's almost overwhelming (but in a good way). There's never nothing to do, and I don't ever feel bored while playing it. While gardening is a good portion of it, you can also fish and go mining, and collect things to sell or keep. 

The aesthetic of the game is very pleasing, and the music is perfect and fits the game nicely. I find a lot of the time that I play Stardew, that I can relax and have a good time. But it also has lots of difficulty too. Like you have to know what items are worth more to sell, where to find everything, and when going to a mine, you have to keep track of your health or you may die! Not only that, you also have to focus on energy, too, which can be depleted by most things you do in-game. This makes it more fun, and spices things up. It also helps those who want something more intense to do!

You can also own animals, as well as pets, and have bonds with them! This is another great feature as it makes things feel more personal and customized. Let alone the fact you can get married and have kids, too! The game makes you feel like you're a part of a community, and these aspects (along with the others mentioned), just makes it feel more rewarding and satisfying.

This is a game where you don't even need mods to enjoy (though there are some amazing ones that I'm sure would make it even better), and while there are some frustrating things--such as the days going so quick--it doesn't dampen the fun you can have in this game. Overall, with all that I mentioned (and the stuff I didn't), this game is very worth giving a shot!

positive.original:
I have never been naturally drawn to pixel art games. The visual style usually makes it harder for me to feel invested. However, I have always loved farming games, and Harvest Moon Back to Nature shaped a significant part of my childhood. I spent a large amount of my primary school years playing it.

Stardew Valley stands out as a modern masterpiece in this genre. Once the game draws you in, the pixel art becomes secondary. The strength of Stardew Valley is how effectively it integrates farming, exploration, character relationships, and progression systems. It brings together everything I wished HM BTN could have expanded on, while still respecting the charm and simplicity of classic farming titles.

The inclusion of multiplayer is a major advantage. It allows for cooperative play and makes the game more accessible for me to share with my child. This flexibility adds depth without compromising the core experience. The ongoing support from the developer is also remarkable. Continuous updates, thoughtful improvements, and the clear passion behind the project elevate the game far beyond standard expectations. I genuinely appreciate the developer, his partner, and every individual involved in making this game what it is.

At this point, I have found very little to criticise. A less blocky visual option would be a welcome addition, but it is not essential. The pixel art style has its own identity and contributes to the atmosphere in a meaningful way.

Overall, Stardew Valley succeeds not only as a farming game, but as a deeply crafted, well-balanced experience that rewards time, curiosity, and care.

positive.original:
In the annals of rustic diversion and pastoral delight, there existeth a singular creation of notable charm and quiet profundity, known unto the modern age as Stardew Valley. This electronic contrivance, though fashioned in an era of advanced artifices, doth summon the spirit of simpler times, wherein the labours of the field and the fellowship of a close-knit village did form the essence of a life well-lived. It is with due reverence and studied contemplation that one may examine the manifold virtues of this most commendable game.

At its commencement, the participant is cast as an inheritor of neglected lands, once tended with care, yet now fallen into disrepair. This inheritance, bestowed by a departed grandsire, doth serve as both burden and opportunity. The soil lieth fallow, the structures crumbleth, and yet within such decay resideth the promise of renewal. Thus beginneth the noble endeavour of cultivation, whereby the player must, through diligence and foresight, restore vitality unto the land.

The act of husbandry, though simple in its outward appearance, revealeth itself to be of intricate design. Seeds must be chosen with wisdom, for each season bringeth forth its own bounty and demandeth its own sacrifices. The tilling of earth, the watering of crops, and the eventual harvest thereof are tasks that, whilst repetitive, instil a curious satisfaction. Therein lieth a reflection of life itself, wherein persistence and patience yield fruits most gratifying.

Yet Stardew Valley is not solely a tale of soil and seed. It is, in equal measure, a study of community and human connexion. The village, quaint and unassuming, is inhabited by a diverse assembly of souls, each possessed of distinct character and temperament. Through acts of kindness, the offering of gifts, and the simple courtesy of conversation, bonds may be forged. Friendships blossom, rivalries soften, and, in some instances, love itself may take root.

The passage of time within this world is marked by the turning of seasons, each bearing its own visage and atmosphere. Spring awakeneth the land with gentle rains and budding life; summer bestoweth warmth and abundance; autumn painteth the fields in hues of gold and crimson; and winter bringeth a hush of snow and introspection. This cyclical nature imparteth a rhythm that governeth all endeavours, urging the player to plan with care and to cherish each fleeting moment.

Moreover, the game extendeth its diversions beyond the confines of agriculture. The adventurous spirit may descend into caverns, wherein lurketh both treasure and peril. Fishing in tranquil waters, foraging in the wilderness, and crafting implements of utility further enrich the experience. Such variety ensureth that monotony findeth no lasting foothold, and that each day presenteth new choices and possibilities.

Of particular note is the aesthetic presentation of Stardew Valley, which employeth a style both modest and evocative. The visual form, rendered in pixels, doth nonetheless convey a richness of detail and emotion. The music, gentle and melodious, accompanieth the player’s journey with a grace that stirreth the heart. Together, these elements createth an atmosphere of serenity seldom matched in works of its kind.

One must also commend the spirit in which this game was brought into being. It standeth as a testament to the vision and perseverance of its creator, who, through singular effort, hath fashioned a work of enduring appeal. Such dedication is mirrored in the experience itself, wherein the player is likewise encouraged to invest time and care into the shaping of their virtual existence.

In contemplation of all these facets, it becometh evident that Stardew Valley is more than mere pastime. It is an ode to the virtues of simplicity, a meditation upon labour and reward, and a celebration of community. In an age oft consumed by haste and distraction, it offereth a gentle reminder of the joys to be found in patience, in routine, and in the quiet cultivation of one’s surroundings.

Thus, in conclusion, one may assert with confidence that Stardew Valley is indeed a game of uncommon merit. Its harmonious blending of mechanics, aesthetics, and thematic depth rendereth it worthy of both admiration and enduring regard. Whosoever seeketh solace in a world of gentle endeavour and heartfelt connexion would do well to partake in its offerings, for therein lieth an experience both enriching and profoundly agreeable.

positive.original:
Genuielly the coziest game I've played in a long time. For me, someone with major ADHD, it does take me keeping a list on my phone so that I can stay on track, but its such an amazing game, its so much fun, the graphics are amazing, and its just over so much fun.
For me, I love the marriage graphics as well, everytime I got for Harvey, he is the sweetest! I also really like the range of quests and characters, it helps the game be more immersive. Some games I've played have minimal quests and its easy and quick, but this challenges you, it also gives you a big range of time to finish it all. I also love how you can choose what you like to do most, mining, foraging, fishing, farming, completing quests, getting full hearts with everyone, etc.
ANYWAYS, I love the games and totally recommend it to someone who likes cozy games but also likes a bit of range and challenge.

TIPS IF YOU BOUGHT THE GAME: 
- Go to the cindersap forest every Friday and Sunday with money, towards the pink tree/secret forrest there is a cart that can help you finish the community center/help you buy things.
- Check the Stardew Valley WIKI for help, it has info on everything, from Fish to Foraging to Characters.
- If you friend certain characters they will send you things in the mail (I can't remember the characters but look it up on google or youtube)
- Cooking Lady is on the TV every Wednesday (Re-Run) and Sunday. She teaches you new recipes and can really help
- If you're going into the mines, pack high energy foods, you will get lower energy and not be able to finish automatically.
- Giving presents on characters birthdays majorly boosts friendship points
- Finish the community center earlier on, it may not seem important but trust me, it is, it unlocks a lot of important/helpful quests (Like Willy's Boat) and finishing bundles helps a lot (Like with the greenhouse, minecarts, bus to the desert, the quarry, etc.)

Some games I've played have minimal quests and its easy and quick, but this challenges you, it also gives you a big range of time to finish it all. I also love how you can choose what you like to do most, mining, foraging, fishing, farming, completing quests, getting full hearts with everyone, etc.
ANYWAYS, I love the games and totally recommend it to someone who likes cozy games but also likes a bit of range and challenge.

TIPS IF YOU BOUGHT THE GAME: 
- Go to the cindersap forest every Friday and Sunday with money, towards the pink tree/secret forrest there is a cart that can help you finish the community center/help you buy things.
- Check the Stardew Valley WIKI for help, it has info on everything, from Fish to Foraging to Characters.
- If you friend certain characters they will send you things in the mail (I can't remember the characters but look it up on google or youtube)
- Cooking Lady is on the TV every Wednesday (Re-Run) and Sunday. She teaches you new recipes and can really help
- If you're going into the mines, pack high energy foods, you will get lower energy and not be able to finish automatically.
- Giving presents on characters birthdays majorly boosts friendship points
- Finish the community center earlier on, it may not seem important but trust me, it is, it unlocks a lot of important/helpful quests (Like Willy's Boat) and finishing bundles helps a lot (Like with the greenhouse, minecarts, bus to the desert, the quarry, etc.)

positive.original:
As someone who usually plays games like DOOM, ULTRAKILL, and The Binding of Isaac, I never thought a farming game would appeal to me, but I was completely wrong.

Stardew Valley is so much more than just farming. There’s an incredible amount of variety, and it genuinely makes me feel happy when I play. The characters are a huge part of that. Each one has their own personality, dialogue, and routines, which makes the town feel alive instead of lifeless like most NPCs in other games.

What really surprised me is how much it feels like a life simulator. Every in-game day has purpose. One day you might spend time in the mines, another fishing, doing farm work, completing quests, or attending festivals. There’s always something to do, and the constant decision-making makes each day feel meaningful.

I also love how the characters don’t just stand around waiting for you. They have their own schedules, hobbies, and lives, which makes the world feel real.

I haven’t fully completed the game yet, but I’ve played enough to confidently say that I love it. This game completely changed my expectations of what a “farming game” could be.

That means I've known about this game and been excited for it for 12 years now. Until just this week though, I have not truly played the game. I would pick it up for an hour here and there and man, the years sure went by...so glad after all this time to actually start a real playthrough. An amazing game, top three right next to the greats like Minecraft and Terraria.

positive.original:
120 hours on Switch version, 100+ hours on PS4 version; So returning player here.

Stardew Valley is the ultimate "Low Cortisol" game. Addictive gameplay loop that consists of farming, foraging, mining, socializing, crafting and even some combat (although not the focus of the game).

Slap one of the best soundtracks in gaming history onto the above and you have yourself one of the most endearing, relaxing and fun farming sims ever.

And Pennie is best girl BTW.

positive.original:
This game is both - it keeps you stressed while being in a cave without better equipment (or go fishing )and is super cozy - taking care of animals, having a relationship, watering the plants and decorating the farm.

It is great if you want to play a game with different type of gamers, becuase you can switch between their play styles, join them and sometimes just seperate so you can just do you. 

It's great for it's simplicity. It looks like a little game, but the lore is huge. There are even apps to help you out how to receive something, how to make your relationship better (for example giving Abi the whole time stones) and how to make money and defeat the evil corperation. 

If you don't don't what game you should play next with your friends, because they are way to different for their playstyles, give Stardew Valley a try.

positive.original:
After 65 hours, I can safely say that Stardew Valley is more than just a farming simulator; it’s a masterpiece of game design. What starts as a simple task of clearing weeds and planting parsnips quickly evolves into a deeply rewarding loop of exploration, friendship, and discovery.

What I love: 
[b] The Atmosphere [/b]: The changing seasons and the incredible soundtrack make every day in-game feel unique.
[b] Depth [/b]: There is always something to do, whether it’s reaching the bottom of the mines, finishing the Community Center, or mastering the art of fishing.
[b] Character Growth [/b]: The NPCs aren't just background noise; they have real stories and struggles that make you feel like part of a community.

It’s the perfect game to unwind with after a long day. If you’re looking for a world to get lost in, this is it.

positive.original:
Played it once before for about 10 minutes and I did not even attempt to like it or care about any aspect of what the game has to offer. Almost 10 years later as a 26 year old male who struggles with panic disorder and multiple other mental health diagnosis, this game is helping me a lot. I've played games since as long as I can remember, as my family are gamers. WoW being one of my top 5 played in my lifetime. I feel like since 2020-2021ish the gaming community has been so focused on fast paced games of all sorts that are online with others and are filled with micro transactions, and battle passes; which is a time many of us will hold near and dear to our hearts. Such as CoD MW rereleasing and being there for most of us during the pandemic. Although, Stardew offers something that I have totally forgotten existed. Something that is your own experience all the way through. There is not a group of players rushing you to get something done, press the right button, or even complete a certain task. Stardew has somehow reminded me how important it is in daily life to slow the ♥♥♥♥ down. I am still very new to the game, unlike many of you. Although I now keep finding myself wanting to come back. I find myself wanting to fish and find out who needs my help next. I am not the biggest fan of the fact that its pokemon style traveling and interactions; but through the few things I personally dislike, there are SO many more to appreciate about this game and the community. I don't really find myself leaving reviews or speaking much especially about things like this as opinions are opinions, but this game deserves the love it gets. I am really excited to see what else the game has to offer, especially the dungeon crawling aspect.
Side note; if anyone wants to adopt a new player please feel free to add me! I'd love to learn more.

negative.original:
Tldr;
Wiki-game. Look up everything.
Punishes your ignorance rather than rewarding your curiosity.
Frustrating rather than relaxing.
Induces "fear of missing out" while pressing deadlines over your head.

I would recommend the game due to the general fun there is, but it feels like a game you’re supposed to have a wiki next to you to enjoy, despite me trying to avoid that until I get too tired of the pressing ingame deadlines and dates to keep up with to have more than just watering my crops.
Simply put- there’s too many "gotcha, try again next year" moments and small annoyances to make this game relaxing and not just annoying to play.

Want an example? A small assignment, get 20 copper ore.
Earlier assignments allow you to use items you found before, but for this specific job you can’t use the 80 copper ore you had mined before. You need NEW copper ore. Could’ve been worded better or been very explicit rather than "bring 20 copper ore".

Another example? Giving villagers gifts is a pain in the ass too. They don’t like a gift? They’ll take it anyway, say "I hate it! Don’t give me gifts!" like a toddler having a tantrum and practically speaking, throw it on the ground to spite you rather than to say no thanks and refuse it.
Why can’t I straight up slap the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ after that level of disrespect? The relaxing baby game feels more like a drama town simulator.

Also, long term saves will not make much sense because the villagers will never change or age.

Another, different criticism is about villagers never bothering to initiate conversation with you- except for business owners trying to sell you ♥♥♥♥.
"Come buy new seeds! Buy my furniture!"
I like Willy at least. That guy gives you a free fishing rod and just shares with you his love for fishing.

The villagers are realistic in a sense, but moreso boring and the lack of interaction makes not only the characters feel shallow but the social game as well, as they will only say the same lines everyday.

Like I get it, Penny works as a teacher, Shane works a depressing job at Joja and hates you and so on- they will never bother to get to know you, they only care if you, the new guy showers them in gifts they specifically like (which you would never find out about without trial and error, hence the wikipedia game label)

Another example? Giving villagers gifts is a pain in the ass too. They don’t like a gift? They’ll take it anyway, say "I hate it! Don’t give me gifts!" like a toddler having a tantrum and practically speaking, throw it on the ground to spite you rather than to say no thanks and refuse it.
Why can’t I straight up slap the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ after that level of disrespect? The relaxing baby game feels more like a drama town simulator.

Also, long term saves will not make much sense because the villagers will never change or age.

Another, different criticism is about villagers never bothering to initiate conversation with you- except for business owners trying to sell you ♥♥♥♥.
"Come buy new seeds! Buy my furniture!"
I like Willy at least. That guy gives you a free fishing rod and just shares with you his love for fishing.

The villagers are realistic in a sense, but moreso boring and the lack of interaction makes not only the characters feel shallow but the social game as well, as they will only say the same lines everyday.

Like I get it, Penny works as a teacher, Shane works a depressing job at Joja and hates you and so on- they will never bother to get to know you, they only care if you, the new guy showers them in gifts they specifically like (which you would never find out about without trial and error, hence the wikipedia game label)

negative.original: Stardew Valley is honestly overrated. Don’t get me wrong, it’s not a bad game at all, but it’s incredibly shallow. Once you finish it once, there’s really no strong reason to keep going. The loop starts repeating itself and there’s not much depth beyond the first full playthrough. I have more hours than I normally would because it’s one of the few games my girlfriend plays, so we spent some time on it together — otherwise I probably would’ve dropped it much earlier.

negative.original:
Tldr;
Wiki-game. Look up everything.
Punishes your ignorance rather than rewarding your curiosity.
Frustrating rather than relaxing.
Induces "fear of missing out" while pressing deadlines over your head.

I would recommend the game due to the general fun there is, but it feels like a game you’re supposed to have a wiki next to you to enjoy, despite me trying to avoid that until I get too tired of the pressing ingame deadlines and dates to keep up with to have more than just watering my crops.
Simply put- there’s too many "gotcha, try again next year" moments and small annoyances to make this game relaxing and not just annoying to play.

Want an example? A small assignment, get 20 copper ore.
Earlier assignments allow you to use items you found before, but for this specific job you can’t use the 80 copper ore you had mined before. You need NEW copper ore. Could’ve been worded better or been very explicit rather than "bring 20 copper ore".

Another example? Giving villagers gifts is a pain in the ass too. They don’t like a gift? They’ll take it anyway, say "I hate it! Don’t give me gifts!" like a toddler having a tantrum and practically speaking, throw it on the ground to spite you rather than to say no thanks and refuse it.
Why can’t I straight up slap the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ after that level of disrespect? The relaxing baby game feels more like a drama town simulator.

Also, long term saves will not make much sense because the villagers will never change or age.

Another, different criticism is about villagers never bothering to initiate conversation with you- except for business owners trying to sell you ♥♥♥♥.
"Come buy new seeds! Buy my furniture!"
I like Willy at least. That guy gives you a free fishing rod and just shares with you his love for fishing.

The villagers are realistic in a sense, but moreso boring and the lack of interaction makes not only the characters feel shallow but the social game as well, as they will only say the same lines everyday.

Like I get it, Penny works as a teacher, Shane works a depressing job at Joja and hates you and so on- they will never bother to get to know you, they only care if you, the new guy showers them in gifts they specifically like (which you would never find out about without trial and error, hence the wikipedia game label)

That said, it ultimately comes down to personal preference, and the gameplay style just isn’t for me.

negative.original:
[h1]Mixed feelings about this one... [/h1]

This is my first life sim game I've played, and perhaps some of my critique is applicable to this genre as a whole. 
I'll start off by saying this game has insane quality of life issues (mainly NPC related). I haven't in my life played a game that needed that many QoL mods like this one. I would never play this game unmodded. 
A lot of the gameplay is just walking from place to place, doing chores, and you could argue that this is what life sim games are about, but what's the point if it's not fun?

It's the type of game I'd play while binge-watching House M.D., and it's definitely not entertaining enough on its own.

This is my first life sim game I've played, and perhaps some of my critique is applicable to this genre as a whole. 
I'll start off by saying this game has insane quality of life issues (mainly NPC related). I haven't in my life played a game that needed that many QoL mods like this one. I would never play this game unmodded. 
A lot of the gameplay is just walking from place to place, doing chores, and you could argue that this is what life sim games are about, but what's the point if it's not fun?

It's the type of game I'd play while binge-watching House M.D., and it's definitely not entertaining enough on its own.

negative.original:
I recommend this game if you have a special interest in farming games or are new to gaming as a hobby. But I didn't like it much. Let me explain why. 
-----
While playing I would have waves of enjoyment and boredom. I would do everything i could do, and then like an in-game week later will unlock a new thing that opens up the world a whole lot more. Having the world open up so often is a really awesome feeling, but it could have better pacing so I'm not bored waiting for the next new thing to get me hooked. I played on keyboard and it was a pretty awful experience control-wise. You gotta like, point vaguely at a direction to interact in that direction, but it's all vibe-based and sometimes just doesnt work at all. I'll be aiming left and my character smacks up. or have my cursor directly on a chest but it opens the chest next to it for no reason. These problems are especially exacerbating to the combat system. At first, the combat was fine for the first 80-90 levels of the Mines as its not taken seriously, the monsters are all cute creatures that hardly hurt you, but the later floors, and also the Skull Cavern you unlock later-- just take themselves too seriously. The combat system was not made for anything difficult to be implemented but the developer did so anyway. Another issue I had was that I wished the role-playing elements were stronger. The game starts out as you making your character. I made the character to be a self-insert, but I had very little control over my character's decisions or how I truly present myself as to the other characters. I want to be a homewrecker and date older gentleman >:). but no, the cast is almost entirely college-aged. Sure, theres like, Harvey, but he suspiciously has quite the baby-face going on. I just feel like I'm not the target demographic for the dating pool. Which is okay, but knowing beforehand how queer this game was I was expecting a lot more diversity (Not just talking about age) like for one, I dont think there's a single Asian in the game. and only one descriptively non-Caucasian dateable character? It's a shame. That's actually not completely true based on technicality, but would require spoilers to explain. This next issue may be a bit of a personal issue as I talked to my friends who have played this game, and while they have had issues, never to the extent of I had. but i had TONS of glitches in my playthrough. My save file got corrupted like 4 times in my 80 hours of playtime. Luckily, the game keeps yesterday's save as backup when-needed, so I never lost too much. It shouldn't have ever happened though, especially more than once.
+++++
To list out some positives: I think the level progression with skills and crafting and new abilities are all very well paced; the game is extremely QoL friendly, one example I'd like to shoutout is that despite normal chests and big chests being completely different items, you can just place a big chest ontop of a normal chest to upgrade it, keeping the inventory. Absolutely stunning thoughtfulness and every game needs to do this.; The mini-games, while being brutal in difficulty, were very fun to play.; Should be expected since it is majority a farming game, but the farming gameplay loop was fun, and trying to make your farm as optimal as possible can strike the fancy of a lot of people. All the characters have pretty distinct personalities, all of them had reasons to love them, and reasons to hate them with their character flaws.

Overall, I found the game to be mid and not for me. Still, I might come back to it someday to try out some of the most popular mod(pack)s to see if that makes the experience any bit more enjoyable for me. But mod support isn't native into Steam so I'm not factoring it into my review. 5.5/10

Which is okay, but knowing beforehand how queer this game was I was expecting a lot more diversity (Not just talking about age) like for one, I dont think there's a single Asian in the game. and only one descriptively non-Caucasian dateable character? It's a shame. That's actually not completely true based on technicality, but would require spoilers to explain. This next issue may be a bit of a personal issue as I talked to my friends who have played this game, and while they have had issues, never to the extent of I had. but i had TONS of glitches in my playthrough. My save file got corrupted like 4 times in my 80 hours of playtime. Luckily, the game keeps yesterday's save as backup when-needed, so I never lost too much. It shouldn't have ever happened though, especially more than once.
+++++
To list out some positives: I think the level progression with skills and crafting and new abilities are all very well paced; the game is extremely QoL friendly, one example I'd like to shoutout is that despite normal chests and big chests being completely different items, you can just place a big chest ontop of a normal chest to upgrade it, keeping the inventory. Absolutely stunning thoughtfulness and every game needs to do this.; The mini-games, while being brutal in difficulty, were very fun to play.; Should be expected since it is majority a farming game, but the farming gameplay loop was fun, and trying to make your farm as optimal as possible can strike the fancy of a lot of people. All the characters have pretty distinct personalities, all of them had reasons to love them, and reasons to hate them with their character flaws.

Overall, I found the game to be mid and not for me. Still, I might come back to it someday to try out some of the most popular mod(pack)s to see if that makes the experience any bit more enjoyable for me. But mod support isn't native into Steam so I'm not factoring it into my review. 5.5/10

negative.original:
I have come to a conclusion and to terms with said conclusion that I do not like this game. It's slow paced and requires my full attention but isn't really distracting and thus I can't truly focus on it. It's full of tasks with short deadlines that aren't fun nor very rewarding and the long-term goal is very vague, heck, an entire day in-game feels like a chore with a deadline, you wake up, pick up carrots, get a quest to deliver a single grape to someone whose name you recognise but don't remember who they are or where they live so you need to look it up, you get 5 coins in return, go fish, catch one, well now the day is ending so you quickly run back home, now your energy is low, too bad you passed out, pay up a fine and on the next day your energy is lower so you can do even less
This game should be one of the tests for ADHD because it feels like a personal hell for a person with ADHD

negative.original:
[h1]Not for Everyone Despite the Hype[/h1]

Despite having an “Overwhelmingly Positive” rating, Stardew Valley is simply not my cup of tea.

The controls feel a bit clunky, and the overall pace is too slow for my taste. The daily energy system, which limits how much you can do each day, makes the experience feel restrictive rather than relaxing.

I used to play Harvest Moon back when I was a teenager, and from what I remember, it felt much less limiting. Maybe that’s just nostalgia talking—but the difference in how it feels is noticeable to me.

I can’t point to one specific reason why the game didn’t click, but it just never felt engaging enough to keep me interested.

Don’t blindly buy it just because of the overwhelming positive reviews—this is one of those games that really depends on personal taste.

negative.original:
Clint is a male character who doesn’t contribute financially but instead uses his physical strength to seize players’ rewards; he claims to be pursuing his writing career but is actually harassing women—and he is a romanceable character.
The romanceable female characters are all friendly, gentle, beautiful, and young; even the only exception, Haley, is portrayed as a “bad girl” rather than a character with room for growth.
The romanceable male characters, on the other hand, vary in age and personality; they possess more flaws and a clear arc of personal growth, and they don’t need to be instantly appealing to players from the very first encounter.
As for the ratio of female to male NPCs, their functional roles, and age diversity—there’s no need to elaborate further. Female NPCs are either friendly, pretty “exotic eye candy,” dutiful wives, or characters waiting to be rescued by the default male player.

Clint is a male character who doesn’t contribute financially but instead uses his physical strength to seize players’ rewards; he claims to be pursuing his writing career but is actually harassing women—and he is a romanceable character.
The romanceable female characters are all friendly, gentle, beautiful, and young; even the only exception, Haley, is portrayed as a “bad girl” rather than a character with room for growth.
The romanceable male characters, on the other hand, vary in age and personality; they possess more flaws and a clear arc of personal growth, and they don’t need to be instantly appealing to players from the very first encounter.
As for the ratio of female to male NPCs, their functional roles, and age diversity—there’s no need to elaborate further. Female NPCs are either friendly, pretty “exotic eye candy,” dutiful wives, or characters waiting to be rescued by the default male player.

negative.original:
[h1]Not for Everyone Despite the Hype[/h1]

Despite having an “Overwhelmingly Positive” rating, Stardew Valley is simply not my cup of tea.

The controls feel a bit clunky, and the overall pace is too slow for my taste. The daily energy system, which limits how much you can do each day, makes the experience feel restrictive rather than relaxing.

I used to play Harvest Moon back when I was a teenager, and from what I remember, it felt much less limiting. Maybe that’s just nostalgia talking—but the difference in how it feels is noticeable to me.

I can’t point to one specific reason why the game didn’t click, but it just never felt engaging enough to keep me interested.

Don’t blindly buy it just because of the overwhelming positive reviews—this is one of those games that really depends on personal taste.

negative.original: What I am starting to find out is that the majority of our video games are not so peaceful. Reddit had many discussions of upset over the mayor or the owner of the seed store reflecting the truth that when faced with a lot of money it sometimes comes down to morals and integrity when faced with vast amounts of wealth. Concerns over Shane in why we cannot keep Jojo Mart, the seed store, and Shane's employment. Why the farm felt like a transfer of property to a spouse or roommate, how gifts felt like a question on whereabouts, or question the death of livestock if a rabbit's foot appeared without explanation while the rabbit was perfectly fine. The world we actually live in is a complicated stressful mess and many of us could utilize a program that is not only peaceful without having to ask too many questions like if the lack of dirt in front of the barns is actually mud. Before I had begun I had no idea what a parsnip was nor had I eaten one but there it sat in the produce section awaiting it's discovery amongst the many veggies yet to be identified and used due to the loss of generational knowledge whether a young mother, foster care, or financial hardships of city life. There is plenty of information still missing such as how farmers choose what to grow as shelf life, prices, and knowing the world has to eat comes into question. We would not have an advanced society where we could work fast food, Information technology, education or factory jobs if it were not for those who grow our food, without them we all would be reduced back to being farmers much like before world war one brought forth industry and an economy that was by far more demanding and quick than what it was when countries harnessed the power of water not only for grinding grain but for spinning string that would later be woven into fabric. Just because the game had proclaimed an ending, it doesn't have to be the ending for I was once told that we do not have to drink the entire beer when we are finished with it as the lessons we had learned was much like finishing what was on the plate or the fuss over the expense in hours worked in the ability of its purchase. It is always good to remember where we came from and that our technological advancements could send us back to the beginning as if it didn't exist in the first place and if so may we remember that we do not have to salt the meat to dry it in salt.

negative.original:
i genuinely never understood how can someone enjoy playing this crap and it's kinda hard for me to explain why too. i tried playing without mods but it's looks ugly as hell, i also don't like the controls for some reason (?) idk. i don't like it with mods either, there's no clothes or hairstyles that look decent enough either in the original game or modded.
i also hate how everytime there's a new "cozy" game that's out and it gets compared to this absolute slop, like "stardew valley but on an island with sea", "stardew valley but you are a magician" etc and all that other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. i don't want to compare it to fields of mistria bc it'll lowkey sound like i'm advertising it, but FoM is quite literally everything i wanted this game to be. this game isn't cozy, the day is too short, it's stupidly complicated at times, like why do i have to look up a characters schedule to get them the ♥♥♥♥ that THEY want, like who do you think you are bro? why do i have to bother wasting time googling schedules and shi to find out i can't even get the said WANTED item to the character in time?"it gets better after 3730 years though!" why do i have to play this for 50+ hours because it's "gets better" in the end and i might not even enjoy what i see after said 3730 years into the game? i regret buying it, but at least it's not 20$ or whatever.
as i also said earlier the mods do not fix anything. before i bought it i saw some mods that looked interesting (that either add portraits that make the ugly azz bachelor/ettes look decent or that add a new interesting character or improve visual, you name it), so i thought about giving it a chance but it's genuinely not worth it. i'd rather play skyrim for 200 times again and it's still more enjoyable and fun.
i can't even put into words how much pure hatred and frustration i have for this game jesus christ man

negative.original:
For a farm game, I expected to be more focused on just farming. You can only hold so many resources even if you have chests and it honestly kills some of the fun of farming if I'm constantly resource shifting. Some of the NPCs are fun but none are to notable. 
I just wanna farm, replant my seeds, and sell my crop to the town but gameplay makes they slog and I honesty can't fall in love with it.
With an hour on here and 6 hours on my console, I just can't past for than 2 seasons before getting bored and never touching it again.
